source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers (2026) ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report
finding: 2025 Kaggle results on ARC-AGI-2 private set: test-time-trained neural models led. The report names test-time training as the source of top scores in both 2024 (ARChitects) and 2025 (NVARC). Program-synthesis refinement loops are the stated theme of 2025.
numbers: 1,455 teams, 15,154 entries. Top scores: NVARC 24.03%, ARChitects 16.53%, MindsAI 12.64%, Lonnie 6.67%, Barbadillo 6.53%. Top cost $0.20 per task.
quote: The central theme driving AGI progress in 2025 is the emergence of the refinement loop.
limits: Read as PDF text. Competition is on ARC-AGI-2. No test of shortest-program selection.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: pure program-length selection did not win the contest. Refinement with a verifier and test-time weight training did.

source: Chollet et al. (2026) ARC Prize 2025 Technical Report: CompressARC, Poetiq harness, reasoning tokens
finding: CompressARC (MDL, no pretraining) won 3rd paper award. Commercial refinement harnesses lift frontier models a lot but cost more. Tasks with a verifier and covered knowledge are called reliably automatable.
numbers: CompressARC: 76K parameters, 20% ARC-AGI-1 eval (20-34% across sets in the award text), 4% on ARC-AGI-2, about 20 min per puzzle on one RTX 4070. Poetiq harness on Gemini 3 Pro: 31% at $0.81 per task to 54% at $31 per task on ARC-AGI-2; Claude Opus 4.5 about $60 per task. Gemini 3 Pro used 96 reasoning tokens vs Deep Think 138,000 on one ARC-1 task.
quote: pure test-time optimization based on description length minimization can solve abstract reasoning tasks
limits: The Poetiq figures are reported by Poetiq; ARC Prize verified the Gemini run. The report does not analyse MDL scaling.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: MDL at test time works but falls from about 20% (ARC-1) to 4% (ARC-2). It helps on simple repeated structure and is not shown to scale. Verifier-driven refinement bought 23 points at about 38x cost.

source: Jolicoeur-Martineau (2025) Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks (TRM)
finding: A 7M-parameter recursive network trained only on the task data with heavy augmentation beats most prompted reasoning LLMs on ARC. Plain direct prediction by a network is much worse.
numbers: TRM-Att 7M: ARC-1 44.6%, ARC-2 7.8%. HRM 27M: 40.3 / 5.0. Direct pred 27M: 21.0 / 0.0. Deepseek R1: 15.8 / 1.3. Claude 3.7 16K: 28.6 / 0.7. o3-mini-high: 34.5 / 3.0. Gemini 2.5 Pro 32K: 37.0 / 4.9. Grok-4-thinking 1.7T: 66.7 / 16.0.
quote: TRM obtains 45% test-accuracy on ARC-AGI-1 and 8% on ARC-AGI-2
limits: Not an MDL method. Uses 1000 augmentations per task. Tuned frontier giants (Bespoke Grok-4, 79.6 / 29.4) still beat it.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: small test-time-trained models are competitive but their gain does not come from a length penalty. Do not credit compression for it.

source: Chollet, Knoop et al. (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: ARC-AGI-2 was built to resist brute-force program search. Reasoning models and the 2024 winners drop to near zero on it.
numbers: Semi-private set, May 2025 (ARC-1 / ARC-2): o3 medium 53.0 / 3.0; ARChitects 56.0 / 2.5; o4-mini 41.8 / 2.4; o3-mini high 34.5 / 3.0; Icecuber 17.0 / 1.6; o1-pro low 23.3 / 0.9; Claude 3.7 8K 21.2 / 0.9. Every ARC-2 task solved by at least 2 non-expert humans; 66% of attempted test pairs solved by humans.
limits: Human panel was not incentivised like models; scores are semi-private.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 3: DSL search (Icecuber) and prompted reasoning models both fall to 1-3% when tasks resist memorised patterns. Program sampling alone is not enough.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2025) Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis: A Case Study on ARC-AGI (SOAR)
finding: Many LLM-written programs are run on the example pairs and on the test input. Programs vote for their output grid, each weighted by its example accuracy. This vote leaves a gap to the oracle that a better selector could close.
numbers: 6k candidate programs per task (3k sampled, 3k refined). Vote vs oracle (any program right) gap averages 9.5 points across models. All-model vote 52.00% on ARC test, oracle 57.25%. Sample-only 3k 29.67% vs Sample&Refine 42.67-42.88% on ARC-train for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (6k budget).
quote: majority voting is not an ideal aggregation strategy
limits: Selector is a weighted vote, not shortest program. No length baseline run.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the vote is the practical baseline and it sits 5 to 10 points below oracle. A length rule has room to help, but nobody has tested it against this vote.

source: Pourcel et al. (2025) SOAR: refinement and hindsight learning
finding: Fine-tuning on the model's own search traces raises both sampling and refinement. Refinement without any weight update already beats plain sampling by about 13 points.
numbers: Iterated self-improvement on ARC-train: +27% (7B), +24% (14B), +20% (32B), +19% (72B) tasks solved. Test-time: 72B goes 25.62% to 44.87%; Mistral-Large-2 26.25% to 45.5%.
limits: The largest gains need fine-tuning; this is not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: execution-checked program search with refinement is strong, but the test-time gains again use weight updates, so a prompt-only router is not shown.

source: Liu, Xia, Wang, Zhang (2023) Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? (EvalPlus)
finding: Programs that pass the original few tests often fail extra tests. Adding about 764 generated tests per task to HumanEval cut measured pass rates a lot.
numbers: HumanEval+ has 764.1 tests per task on average (164 tasks). pass@k fell by up to 19.3% (pass@1), 24.9% (pass@10), 28.9% (pass@100). ChatGPT -12.6%, GPT-4 -13.1%, CodeGen-16B -18.5%, CodeLlama-34B -17.6%, StarCoder -14.1%.
limits: 2023 models; task is spec-to-code, not rule induction from examples. Tests are wide-coverage, not mutated examples.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a program fitting a handful of checks fails a wider suite 12-19% of the time at pass@1, and the drop grows with k. Our agent should hold out or mutate inputs before trusting fit.

source: Wang et al. (2025) CodeContests+: High-Quality Test Case Generation for Competitive Programming
finding: Weak test suites accept wrong programs and sometimes reject right ones. More tests raise verifier accuracy.
numbers: In original CodeContests over 4000 problems have TPR <= 0.1 and TNR >= 0.9 (almost all correct submissions marked wrong; bad tests and missing checkers). CodeContests+ 5x has almost twice as many qualified problems as CodeContests; the 1x version has over 80% more with one quarter of the tests.
limits: Competitive programming with human submissions; not LLM rule induction. Gives no per-model false-positive rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: verifier accuracy depends on test count and quality. With 2-5 examples (ARC), fit is weak evidence.

source: Chen et al. (2022) CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
finding: Choosing among many samples by agreement between generated programs and generated tests (dual execution agreement) is a strong selector.
numbers: code-davinci-002 HumanEval pass@1 47.0% to 65.8%, MBPP 58.1% to 67.7%. Codex pass@100 77.4% vs pass@1 33.5% shows the selection gap.
quote: selecting a single correct solution from multiple candidates generated by large language models remains a hard problem
limits: Agreement is a vote-like selector; no length term tested. 2022 model.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: among candidates, consensus selection gives about 19 points. This is the bar a length-based rule has to beat at equal samples.

source: Zhang, Yu, Hashimoto, Lewis, Yih, Fried (2022) Coder-Reviewer Reranking for Code Generation
finding: Ranking samples by the model's own log-probability is biased by length. Plain likelihood prefers short degenerate programs; length-normalising overcorrects to long ones. Adding a reviewer term (probability of the instruction given the program) fixes much of this.
numbers: Coder-Reviewer variants beat the best Coder-only variants in 43 of 48 dataset-by-model pairs (six datasets, eight models).
quote: Coder-only reranking prefers short solutions; applying length normalization overcorrects and prefers long solutions.
limits: 2022 models; uses model likelihood, not a fixed-language length.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 1: model log-probs as a length measure are unsafe. Use a code length computed in a fixed language (token or syntax-tree count), not the LM's own probability.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library Learning Doesn't: The Curious Case of the Single-Use Library
finding: Two published LLM library-learning systems barely reuse their learned tools. Their gains come from self-correction and self-consistency.
numbers: LEGO-Prover: only 1,233 lemmas (6%) reach the final prover; exactly one is reused, once. TroVE: 3 successful reuses in 3,201 test questions (of 15 learned functions, 2 reused). Ablation with no cross-problem sharing solved only 1 question fewer (12-problem subset, 50 attempts, 2 trials, GPT-4o-mini).
quote: rather than reuse, self-correction and self-consistency are the primary drivers
limits: Math domains, two systems, small ablation.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: library gains can be an artefact. Any helper memory in our agent needs a zero-reuse control at equal tokens.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions
finding: A gradient-free library of verified helper functions, learned from about 200 examples, raises program prediction accuracy across five domains.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B absolute gains: +11.5% LOGO, +26.1% date understanding, +8.1% TextCraft. CodeLlama-13B with abstractions beats GPT-3.5 without by 19.2% on one domain. Random curriculum order cost 18.7 points on LOGO. CodeLlama-34B LOGO 22.2 to 30.8.
limits: Token cost of the added library in the prompt is not matched against baselines. No break-even task count.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: helper libraries help with no weight updates when tasks share subroutines (LOGO, dates). Order of tasks matters.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The KoLMogorov Test (ICLR), appendix B: o1-mini and chain of thought
finding: A reasoning model (o1-mini) did not beat GPT-4o on writing the shortest program that reproduces data. Chain of thought gave no real gain.
numbers: Sequences of length 128: o1-mini executable programs 81.7% vs GPT-4o 89.9%; accuracy among executable 69.8 vs 63.2; overall Accuracy 57.2 vs 56.5. o1-mini evaluated on 500 random sub-sequences only.
quote: longer chains-of-thought are able to increase performance, they do not yet lead to major improvements
limits: Only o1-mini (late 2024), 500 subsequences. No o3, Claude or Gemini thinking models tested in the paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly: first sign that reasoning models do not fix compression by code. 2025-2026 frontier models still untested.

source: Huang, Zhang, Shan, He (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly: scope statement
finding: The authors say the compression-benchmark line is measured on base models only, because fine-tuned models are not general-purpose compressors.
numbers: No numbers; scope and limitations sections.
quote: fine-tuned models are no longer general-purpose compressors
limits: They call the fine-tuned case interesting but unstudied. No reasoning-model data.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: likelihood as a quality proxy is licensed only for base models. Not usable to rank an instruct or reasoning model.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2019) The Omniglot challenge: a 3-year progress report
finding: Authors' own restatement of the 2015 Bayesian program learning results plus later neural models. It corrects claim K21: BPL error was 3.3% and humans 4.5%, not the reverse.
numbers: 20-way within-alphabet one-shot classification: humans 4.5% error (upper bound), BPL 3.3%, simple ConvNet 13.5%, Siamese ConvNet 8.0% (augmented). Later nets: 2016-2018 results 13.7% down to 4.0-6.0% depending on background set; BPL 4.3% and 4.0% on the minimal splits.
quote: BPL performs comparably to people, achieving an error rate of 3.3% on one-shot classification
limits: Authors' own report. Original Science paper still not opened (HTTP 403). Neural models later matched or beat BPL on some variants.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: Lake 2015 numbers confirmed second-hand. The program-learning edge shrinks as meta-learned nets improve.

source: Feldman (2000) Minimization of Boolean complexity in human concept learning, Nature 407:630-633
finding: Human difficulty of Boolean concepts rises with the length of the shortest equivalent formula.
numbers: 41 mathematically distinct concept types in six families. Difficulty 'directly proportional' to Boolean complexity. Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC).
quote: the subjective difficulty of a concept is directly proportional to its Boolean complexity
limits: Abstract only. Replication status and effect sizes unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: supports a length penalty in S7 as a human-like default. No LLM comparison found.

source: Planton et al. (2021) A theory of memory for binary sequences: Evidence for a mental compression algorithm in humans, PLoS Comput Biol
finding: Human memory for binary sequences follows the length of the shortest description in a small recursive language, and beats six rival models.
numbers: Five experiments, auditory and visual sequences. The complexity measure predicts ratings and violation detection. Adding it to a transition-probability model cut that model's share of variance.
quote: human sequence coding relies on an internal compression using language-like nested structures
limits: Abstract only. Short binary sequences. The description language was chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: independent evidence that human simplicity tracks code length in a fixed small language, which is what S7 would use.

source: Feldman (2016) The simplicity principle in perception and cognition, WIREs Cognitive Science 7:330-340
finding: Review that frames simplicity as a balance between a bias to simple models and a demand to fit the data.
quote: the mind seeks the simplest available interpretation of observations
agent_relevance: Gap 6: names both terms of the trade-off the selector needs (fit first, then length).
